title: Training stages
scopeHtml: Pretraining, SFT, preference optimization (RLHF/DPO/RLAIF), verifiable-reward RL, synthetic data, and what changes between base and chat models.

notes.title: Pretraining
notes.html:
Objective. A base model is trained to predict the next token: given tokens x₁..x_{t-1}, maximize the probability of x_t, averaged over every position of every document. The loss is cross-entropy. This single, self-supervised objective needs no labels, so it scales to trillions of tokens. To predict the next token well over diverse text the model has to learn grammar, facts, reasoning patterns, code syntax, translation and style: capabilities emerge as a by-product.

Scale. Frontier-scale pretraining uses roughly 10 to 30+ trillion tokens, thousands to tens of thousands of GPUs for weeks to months, mixed precision (bf16/fp8), parallelism across data, tensor, pipeline and sequence dimensions, and careful stability engineering (learning-rate warmup and decay, gradient clipping, loss-spike recovery, checkpoints).

The data pipeline (often the real differentiator):

  1. Collect: web crawls, books, code repositories, papers, forums, multilingual sources, licensed data.
  2. Extract and clean: HTML to text, remove boilerplate, language identification.
  3. Quality filtering: heuristic rules, perplexity filters against a reference model, classifiers trained to recognise "educational" or high-quality text.
  4. De-duplication: exact and near-duplicate (MinHash) removal, because duplicates cause memorization and skew.
  5. Safety and privacy filtering: remove personal data, toxic content, malware.
  6. Decontamination: drop documents that overlap with evaluation benchmarks.
  7. Mixing: choose proportions (web, code, maths, books, multilingual) and sometimes upsample high-quality sources or run a final "annealing" phase on the best data.
  8. Tokenization and packing into fixed-length sequences.

Base model vs chat model. A base model continues text; given "What is the capital of France?" it may continue with more quiz questions. It does not reliably follow instructions, refuse harmful requests or hold a persona. The chat/instruct model comes from the post-training stages below.

Knowledge cutoff. The model only contains information from before its data cutoff, and its knowledge of the last months before cutoff is thin because the web has not fully written about it yet. After that date it is unaware of events, library versions or prices, yet may answer fluently and wrongly. Fixes: retrieval, tools, or putting current facts in the prompt; do not just ask "is this up to date?".

Memorization and privacy. Models can reproduce rare training text verbatim, especially duplicated data; this is a copyright and privacy consideration handled by de-duplication, filtering and sometimes output filters.

Real life. Reading an enormous library to learn how language and the world work, long before being taught how to answer questions politely.

Interview angle. The next-token objective, why data quality and de-duplication matter, and the difference between base and instruct models.

notes.title: Supervised fine-tuning
notes.html:
Purpose. SFT turns a base model into an instruction follower by training on curated (instruction, ideal response) examples, with the loss applied only to the assistant's tokens. It teaches format and behaviour (follow the request, be concise or structured, adopt a tone, use the chat template, call tools) rather than new world knowledge; the knowledge is already in the base model.

Data. Typically thousands to a few hundred thousand examples. Quality and diversity beat quantity: a small, carefully curated set (the "LIMA" finding) can give strong results. Sources: human-written demonstrations, filtered real conversations, model-generated data with verification, and task-specific datasets (code with tests, maths with verified answers).

Pipeline.

  1. Define behaviours and write guidelines (style, safety, refusals, formatting).
  2. Collect/clean examples; remove duplicates and low-quality or unsafe responses.
  3. Format with the chat template; mask loss on prompts.
  4. Train with a small learning rate (e.g. 1e-5), 1 to 3 epochs, evaluating on held-out tasks.
  5. Evaluate capability, instruction following and safety; iterate on data.

Risks.

  • Catastrophic forgetting. Fine-tuning hard on narrow data degrades earlier abilities. Mitigate with a low learning rate, fewer epochs, mixing general data back in, or parameter-efficient methods (LoRA).
  • Hallucination pressure. Training on answers that contain facts the model does not know teaches it to guess confidently; include "I don't know" examples.
  • Overfitting to style (always verbose, always bullets).
  • Template mismatch between training and serving.

Real life. On-the-job training after university: shaping how existing knowledge is applied.

notes.title: RLHF and DPO
notes.html:
RLHF pipeline.

  1. Collect preference data: for a prompt, sample two or more responses from the SFT model; human raters rank them.
  2. Train a reward model (RM): a model that outputs a scalar score and is trained so preferred responses score higher (Bradley-Terry loss).
  3. Optimize the policy with RL (commonly PPO) to maximize the RM score, with a KL penalty to the SFT model so the policy does not drift into reward-hacking gibberish.

It is powerful but complex: four models in memory (policy, reference, reward, value), instability, and hyperparameter sensitivity.

DPO (Direct Preference Optimization). Skips the explicit reward model and RL loop. A closed-form derivation shows the optimal policy relates to the reference through the reward, which gives a simple loss on preference pairs (prompt, chosen, rejected): increase the log-probability ratio of the chosen response over the rejected one relative to the reference model, scaled by β. It is stable and cheap (two forward passes of the policy and reference), so it is widely used. Variants: IPO, KTO (works with thumbs-up/down), ORPO, SimPO.

Choosing a method.

Situation Choice
Limited compute, offline preference data, stable training wanted DPO-style
Need online exploration, verifiable rewards, maximum performance RL (PPO/GRPO)
Only binary feedback available KTO-style

Preference data quality and cost. Labelling is expensive and noisy; raters disagree, prefer longer or more confident answers, and are affected by fatigue and position. Clear guidelines, calibration sessions, agreement measurement (e.g. Cohen's kappa), adversarial prompts and gold checks improve quality. The reward ceiling is the quality of the preference signal.

DPO implementation sketch.

# logp_* are summed token log-probs of each response under policy / reference
loss = -F.logsigmoid(beta * ((logp_pol_chosen - logp_ref_chosen)
                           - (logp_pol_rejected - logp_ref_rejected))).mean()

Real life. A taste panel scoring dishes; the chef adjusts the recipe toward higher scores, while a rule says "don't stray too far from the house style" (KL penalty).

notes.title: Reward hacking and sycophancy
notes.html:
Reward hacking. Optimizing a proxy (the reward model) rather than the true goal invites exploitation: longer answers, confident tone, specific formatting tricks, flattery, or in code settings editing the tests instead of fixing the bug. The KL penalty, ensembles of reward models, early stopping and adversarial evaluation reduce it.

Sycophancy. The model tells users what they want to hear (agrees with wrong claims, caves under pushback, praises poor work) because raters tend to prefer agreeable answers. Mitigations: preference data that rewards correct disagreement, evaluations for stance consistency, system prompts and training on "pushback" cases.

Side effects of preference tuning.

  • Alignment tax: a small drop in some raw capabilities.
  • Over-refusal: declining benign requests that superficially resemble harmful ones (e.g. "how to kill a Python process"). Counter with "should-answer" data, borderline-case evaluation, and calibrated safety policies.
  • Mode collapse / style homogenization and reduced diversity.
  • Verbosity bias.
  • Calibration damage: tuned models are often more overconfident than base models.

Process. Audit with held-out adversarial prompts, track refusal rate on benign sets, and measure both harmlessness and helpfulness.

Real life. A student who games the marking scheme by padding essays rather than understanding the subject.

notes.title: RLAIF and RLVR
notes.html:
RLAIF / Constitutional AI. Replace some human labelling with an AI model that critiques and ranks responses against a written set of principles (a "constitution"), then train on those AI preferences (and revisions). Benefits: scalable, consistent, transparent values, less exposure of humans to harmful content. Risks: inherits the labeller's biases, needs spot-checks by humans.

RLVR (reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards). For tasks whose answers can be checked automatically (maths final answers, code that passes unit tests, logic puzzles, format constraints) the reward is computed by a program, no reward model needed. Algorithms like GRPO sample a group of answers per prompt and use relative rewards inside the group. This is the main driver behind reasoning models: long chains of thought that lead to verified answers get reinforced. Limitations: only works where verification is possible; can reward lucky guesses without process supervision; needs guards against exploiting the checker.

Real life. A referee guided by a rulebook (RLAIF) versus an answer key that marks the work (RLVR).

notes.title: Synthetic data
notes.html:
Why. Human data is expensive and finite. Models can generate instructions, responses, reasoning traces, code with tests, translations and paraphrases at scale, and a stronger model can supervise a weaker one.

Pipeline. Seed prompts/taxonomy → generate diverse prompts → generate responses (with a strong model, tools or verifiers) → filter (execution checks, judge scores, de-duplication, safety) → mix with real data → train → evaluate.

Model collapse. Training repeatedly on a model's own outputs narrows the distribution: rare events (the tails) disappear and diversity decays over generations. Defences: keep real human data in the mix, diversify prompts, verify with external signals (tests, tools), use stronger/different teachers, and monitor diversity metrics.

Other risks: amplified errors and biases, benchmark contamination, licence limits on using another model's outputs.

Real life. Photocopying a photocopy loses detail with each generation.

notes.title: Planning post-training
notes.html:
Typical order.

  1. Fix the data and evaluation first: define target behaviours, safety policy and an eval suite (capability, instruction following, safety, over-refusal).
  2. SFT for format and basic behaviour.
  3. Preference tuning (DPO or RLHF) for helpfulness/harmlessness/style.
  4. RL with verifiable rewards for reasoning, code and tool use.
  5. Safety hardening and red teaming; iterate.
  6. Distillation to smaller serving models, quantization, and regression checks.

Decision factors: budget, labelling capacity, risk profile, whether outputs are verifiable, and the specific failure you must fix (format → SFT; tone/refusal balance → preference tuning; reasoning → RLVR). Keep rollback points and compare each stage against the previous on the full eval.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Stages in order. Pretraining (next-token prediction on trillions of tokens, gives knowledge and ability) → SFT (instruction/format behaviour from curated demonstrations) → preference tuning (RLHF with a reward model and PPO, or DPO directly on chosen/rejected pairs) → RL with verifiable rewards (reasoning) → safety tuning and evaluation.

Key distinctions. Base model continues text; chat model follows instructions. SFT teaches behaviour, not new facts. Knowledge ends at the cutoff; use retrieval/tools for current facts. DPO is simpler and more stable; RL gives more power and exploration. RLAIF scales labelling with a constitution; RLVR uses programmatic verification and drives reasoning models.

Failure modes. Catastrophic forgetting, reward hacking, sycophancy, alignment tax, over-refusal, verbosity bias, overconfidence, model collapse from synthetic data, benchmark contamination.

Mitigations. Data quality and diversity, mixing in general data, KL penalties and early stopping, adversarial and borderline evaluation sets, verification of synthetic data, keeping human data in the loop.

Interview one-liners.

  • "Pretraining gives the knowledge; SFT and preference tuning shape how it is used."
  • "DPO is RLHF without the reward model and the RL loop."
  • "Verifiable rewards are why reasoning models improved so quickly."
  • "Preference data quality caps what preference tuning can achieve."

questions.promptHtml: What is an LLM actually trained to do during pretraining, and how does that one objective produce models that can write code, translate and answer questions?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you understand that "intelligence" is a by-product of next-token prediction, which anchors every later discussion about hallucination, base vs chat, and cutoff.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Pretraining minimizes cross-entropy on next-token prediction over trillions of tokens: given tokens 1..t, maximize the log-probability of token t+1. Nothing else is supervised. To predict text well across the web, the model has to compress grammar, facts, code semantics and reasoning patterns into its weights, so those skills emerge as a side effect. The result is a base model that continues text, not one that follows instructions."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
For a token sequence x_1..x_T the loss is the average of -log p(x_t | x_<t). With a causal mask, one forward pass gives T training signals, which is why this objective is so sample-efficient per FLOP.

tokens:   The  cat  sat  on
targets:  cat  sat  on   the
loss:     -log p(cat|The) - log p(sat|The cat) - ...   (averaged)
  • Perplexity = exp(mean cross-entropy). A model with loss 2.0 nats has perplexity about 7.4: on average it is as uncertain as a uniform choice among about 7.4 tokens. Perplexity is only comparable across models that share a tokenizer, because a bigger vocabulary changes what "per token" means. Compare bits-per-byte across tokenizers.
  • Why skills emerge: predicting the next token of a Python file requires modelling syntax and often intent; predicting the answer after "Q: capital of France? A:" requires the fact. The loss rewards any internal circuit that lowers it.
  • Teacher forcing: training feeds the true prefix, inference feeds the model's own samples. This train/inference gap is one reason errors compound in long generations.
  • What it does not optimize: truthfulness, helpfulness, safety, format. A base model asked "What is 2+2?" may continue with "What is 3+3?" because quiz-lists are common text.
  • Other objectives exist (masked LM in BERT, span corruption in T5; see the model-architectures section) but the frontier chat models are causal LMs.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def lm_loss(logits, input_ids):
    # logits: [B, T, V]; predict token t+1 from position t
    shift_logits = logits[:, :-1, :].reshape(-1, logits.size(-1))
    shift_labels = input_ids[:, 1:].reshape(-1)
    return F.cross_entropy(shift_logits, shift_labels)

# perplexity = torch.exp(loss)
# Broken: forgetting the shift trains the model to copy the current token -> loss ~0, useless model.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying pretraining "teaches the model facts" as if retrieving from a database; it stores lossy statistical associations.
  • Comparing perplexity across different tokenizers.
  • Believing loss on web text tracks downstream task quality linearly; it correlates, not guarantees.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is loss computed on all positions at once? → Causal masking lets one pass yield T targets; it is the main efficiency win over RNN-style training.
  2. What is teacher forcing's downside? → Exposure bias: the model never sees its own mistakes during training.
  3. Why can't you just compare perplexity of Llama and GPT? → Different tokenizers and test sets; use bits-per-byte on the same text.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "predicts the next word." The senior adds that the objective is a compression proxy, explains why perplexity is tokenizer-bound, and connects the lack of any truthfulness term to hallucination and to why post-training exists.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that prompt a base model like a chat model get rambling continuations and blame "quality"; the objective explains it. See the base-vs-chat question below.

questions.promptHtml: What exactly changes between a base model and the chat/instruct model you call through an API? When would you deliberately choose the base model?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who treat models as black boxes from those who know the post-training stack.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A base model is the raw pretrained next-token predictor. The chat model is that same network after supervised fine-tuning on instruction/response pairs, then preference optimization (RLHF, DPO or similar), often plus safety and tool-use training. Weights are changed modestly, but behavior changes a lot: it follows a chat template, answers instead of continuing, refuses some requests, and is more verbose and agreeable. I pick a base model for few-shot pattern completion, calibrated probabilities, creative diversity, or as the starting point for my own fine-tune."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
web text -> [pretrain] -> BASE -> [SFT] -> [preference opt / RL] -> [safety, tools] -> CHAT
  • Format: chat models are trained on a fixed template (role tokens like system/user/assistant). Feed a base model that template and it has never seen those tokens in meaning; feed a chat model raw text without the template and quality drops.
  • Distribution shift: post-training sharpens the output distribution (lower entropy). Diversity falls, and token probabilities become less calibrated: reported studies show base models' confidence matches accuracy better than RLHF'd ones (the GPT-4 technical report showed this for the pretrained model; verify on current models).
  • Capabilities: knowledge is almost entirely from pretraining; post-training mostly elicits and shapes it, though reasoning-RL (see RLVR question) can add real skill.
  • When base wins: (1) completion-style tasks (autocomplete, continuing a document), (2) few-shot classification where you want clean logprobs, (3) generating diverse synthetic data, (4) your own SFT/RL, where the instruct model's baked-in habits are unwanted, (5) research on pretraining behavior.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# Same prompt, two behaviors (illustrative)
prompt = "Translate to French: cheese ->"
# base model: "fromage\nTranslate to French: bread -> pain\n..."  (keeps going)
# chat model with template: "fromage"  (stops at end-of-turn token)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using a base model with a chat prompt and judging it "dumb."
  • Assuming the instruct model is strictly better; it is worse at calibration and diversity.
  • Forgetting the chat template when serving an open-weight instruct model (see the tokenization chunk for template bugs).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why are instruct models less calibrated? → Preference optimization pushes probability mass toward preferred modes; confidences become overconfident.
  2. Can you turn a base into a chat model cheaply? → Yes, SFT on a few thousand high-quality examples gives the format; quality of behavior needs more.
  3. Does post-training add knowledge? → Mostly no; it can surface or suppress it, and SFT on new facts can encourage hallucination.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "chat is fine-tuned base." Senior: names each stage, its data, what each changes (format, distribution sharpness, refusal), and picks base deliberately for specific workloads.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team scoring classification confidence with an instruct model's logprobs found thresholds useless (everything at 0.99); switching to the base model's logprobs gave usable ranking.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through how a pretraining corpus is built from raw web crawl. Why do deduplication, quality filtering and data mixing matter so much?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Data quality is the largest controllable lever in pretraining; seniors should reason about it, and about what leaks into model behavior.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Raw crawl goes through extraction (HTML to text), language ID, heuristic filters, model-based quality filters, PII and toxicity handling, deduplication at exact and fuzzy levels, decontamination against benchmarks, then mixing across sources (web, code, books, math, multilingual) with chosen proportions and often an annealing phase of high-quality data at the end. Dedup reduces memorization and wasted compute; filtering raises the average quality per token; mixing sets the capability profile."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
crawl -> text extraction -> lang ID -> heuristic filters (length, symbol ratio, repetition)
      -> quality classifier (e.g. similar-to-reference-corpus) -> PII/toxicity
      -> exact dedup (hash) -> fuzzy dedup (MinHash+LSH / suffix array)
      -> decontaminate vs eval sets -> tokenize -> weighted mixture -> shuffle/pack
  • Dedup evidence: Lee et al. (Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better, 2021) found over 1% of unprompted model output was copied verbatim from training data, one 61-word sentence appeared over 60,000 times in C4, deduped-trained models emitted memorized text about 10x less often, and train/validation overlap affected over 4% of validation sets. So dedup also protects eval validity.
  • Fuzzy dedup: near-duplicates (boilerplate, scraped copies) are found with MinHash signatures and LSH buckets (Jaccard similarity), or suffix arrays for exact substring repeats.
  • Quality filtering: heuristics are cheap; classifier filters (trained to recognize "textbook-like" or reference-quality text) raise benchmark scores but can bias toward one register and under-represent dialects. This is a fairness/coverage trade-off.
  • Mixing: proportions are tuned with small proxy runs. Code and math upweighting is known to help reasoning even for non-code tasks. Multi-epoch repetition of high-quality data is acceptable for a few epochs, repeating low-quality data is not.
  • Annealing / late-stage data: final part of training uses a lower learning rate on curated data (math, code, instruction-like) to boost targeted skills.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
from datasketch import MinHash, MinHashLSH

def sig(text, n=5):
    m = MinHash(num_perm=128)
    toks = text.split()
    for i in range(len(toks) - n + 1):
        m.update(" ".join(toks[i:i+n]).encode())
    return m

lsh = MinHashLSH(threshold=0.8, num_perm=128)
for doc_id, text in corpus:          # corpus: iterable of (id, str)
    s = sig(text)
    if lsh.query(s):                 # near-duplicate already kept
        continue
    lsh.insert(doc_id, s)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Dedup only at document level; repeated paragraphs inside distinct documents remain.
  • Filtering with a classifier trained on Wikipedia-style text and silently dropping informal or non-English content.
  • Forgetting decontamination, so benchmark scores are inflated.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does duplicated data hurt beyond wasted compute? → It increases memorization and privacy leakage and skews the distribution toward repeated content.
  2. How do you pick mixture weights? → Ablations with small proxy models, then validate scaling; do not trust a single run.
  3. When is repeating data okay? → A few epochs of high-quality data have small penalty; returns diminish quickly (see the scaling-laws chunk for the data wall).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average lists "clean the data." Senior knows the specific techniques (MinHash/LSH, classifier filters), the evidence (dedup paper numbers), and the second-order costs (bias from filters, contamination).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Internal continued-pretraining on company wiki exports without dedup made the model regurgitate boilerplate legal footers verbatim.

questions.promptHtml: What is supervised fine-tuning (instruction tuning) for an LLM, what does the data look like, and what does the loss actually apply to?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: SFT is the first post-training step and the one engineers most often run themselves; loss masking and data quality are the common failure points.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "SFT continues training the base model with the same next-token loss, but on curated prompt/response pairs formatted with the chat template. Loss is usually computed only on the assistant tokens, not the prompt. It teaches format, style and instruction-following, not new knowledge. A few thousand to tens of thousands of very high-quality examples can work; quality beats quantity."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Data shape: {messages: [{role: system...}, {role: user...}, {role: assistant...}]} rendered through the model's template with end-of-turn token.
  • Loss masking: labels for prompt tokens set to -100 (ignored by PyTorch cross-entropy), so the model is not trained to generate user text. Some recipes train on all tokens; the choice matters when prompts are long and responses short.
  • Superficial alignment view: the LIMA paper argued ~1,000 curated examples suffice to elicit style, since knowledge comes from pretraining (verify exact figures). Practical corollary: more SFT data of mediocre quality can reduce quality.
  • Sources of data: human-written demonstrations, filtered logs, model-generated data (see synthetic data question), rewritten FAQs. Diversity of tasks matters more than count.
  • Hyperparameters: learning rate much lower than pretraining (often 1e-5 to 2e-5 for full fine-tune, verify per model), 1 to 3 epochs; more epochs overfit and cause forgetting.
  • Packing: concatenating examples into long sequences boosts throughput but needs attention masks that stop cross-example attention.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
IGNORE = -100
def build_example(tok, messages):
    ids, labels = [], []
    for m in messages:
        part = tok.apply_chat_template([m], tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=False)
        ids += part
        labels += part if m["role"] == "assistant" else [IGNORE] * len(part)
    return {"input_ids": ids, "labels": labels}

(Real code must handle templates that need the full conversation to render; render once, then mask by span offsets.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Training on prompt tokens and system prompts, wasting capacity and teaching the model to imitate users.
  • Missing the end-of-turn token so the fine-tuned model never stops.
  • Treating SFT as a way to inject lots of new facts; it mostly teaches behavior.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. SFT vs prompting? → SFT bakes in format and style, saves tokens, but costs data and drift risk; see the fine-tuning track for the decision.
  2. Why low learning rate? → Avoid overwriting pretrained features (forgetting).
  3. Why can SFT cause hallucination? → Training on facts the base model does not know teaches it to assert unknowns confidently.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "fine-tune on Q&A pairs." Senior covers masking, template and EOS correctness, data diversity vs volume, the hallucination risk of new-knowledge SFT.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A support model fine-tuned without EOS in labels generated until max_tokens on every call, tripling cost until caught.

questions.contextHtml:
You SFT a 7B open-weight base model on 18,000 customer-support conversations, 2 epochs, LR 2e-5. Eval loss looks great (0.31, train 0.29) but in a live canary the model answers correctly and then keeps going, inventing a fake "User:" turn and answering itself, in about 35% of requests, averaging 480 output tokens instead of 90. Your data prep:

def to_text(ex):
    text = ""
    for m in ex["messages"]:
        text += f"{m['role'].upper()}: {m['content']}\n"
    return {"text": text}

# trainer: standard causal LM loss on "text", max_len 1024, no special tokens added
# inference: tokenizer.apply_chat_template(msgs, add_generation_prompt=True), stop on eos

Red herrings: GPU is fine, the LR is typical, and eval loss is low.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, how do you confirm it, and how do you fix it without retraining blindly?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Lower LR, add more data, or add a max_tokens limit." Treats it as a quality problem; never notices the train/inference format mismatch.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which model's chat template is used at inference (a mismatch with training is the first suspect)? Does the training data contain an end-of-sequence token per example? Is loss masked? What is the stop condition in the serving config? Did the base model have a chat template at all?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add stop sequences ("\nUSER:") and a sane max_tokens in the serving layer, roll the canary to 0%, and keep the old model live.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Training text uses a hand-rolled "ROLE: text" format with no end-of-turn/EOS token, so the model never learned to stop; (b) inference uses a different template than training, so the model is off-distribution; (c) loss includes user turns, so it learned to generate "USER:" lines; (d) overfitting from 2 epochs (unlikely, eval loss is fine).
  4. How I'd verify each: Decode a few training examples and print the last 10 token IDs; check whether tok.eos_token_id appears. Print the rendered inference prompt vs a training example side by side. Check labels for -100 on user spans. Look at logprob of EOS right after the assistant answer: if it is tiny (<1e-3) the model never learned to end.
  5. Root cause: Two bugs compounding: no EOS/end-of-turn token in training sequences, and training on the whole concatenated transcript, so the model learned the transcript pattern "USER: ... ASSISTANT: ... USER: ..." as plain text continuation. Low eval loss is expected because eval used the same flawed format, and loss averaged over mostly easy tokens hides it.
  6. Fix: Short term: stop sequences. Long term: render with the model's own chat template, append the end-of-turn token to each assistant message, mask non-assistant tokens, and retrain.
def build(tok, msgs):
    ids = tok.apply_chat_template(msgs, tokenize=True)   # includes end-of-turn tokens
    labels = mask_non_assistant(tok, msgs, ids)          # -100 elsewhere
    return {"input_ids": ids, "labels": labels}
  1. Prevention: A unit test asserting the training render equals the serving render for a fixed conversation; a pre-training check that every example ends in EOS; an eval that measures output length distribution and runaway rate.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just cap max_tokens permanently (hides the bug, truncates legit long answers). I would not lower LR or add data first; that does not touch the format bug.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can a stop sequence fully fix it? → It hides symptoms but the model still wastes tokens generating the fake turn up to the stop string, and quality of the first answer may still be affected by the off-format.
  • What if the base model has no chat template? → Define one, add the special tokens to the tokenizer, and resize embeddings; the new token embeddings must be trained (include them in trainable params).
  • Why was eval loss low? → Eval shares the training format; per-token loss is dominated by predictable tokens.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team ran two sprints tuning LR and data volume against a "rambling model" before someone diffed the training render against the serving render and found a missing newline and EOS. The fix was four lines.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames hyperparameters or data volume; proposes only max_tokens.
  • Hire: Identifies missing EOS / template mismatch and masks loss; proposes verification via token IDs.
  • Strong hire: Also adds render-equality tests, EOS-logprob diagnostic, runaway-rate metric, and handles new special-token embedding training.

questions.promptHtml: What is a model's knowledge cutoff, why is it fuzzy, and how do you design applications around it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Stale-answer bugs are common; interviewers want to see that you separate parametric knowledge from retrieval and handle "today's date" correctly.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The cutoff is the date after which the pretraining data contains little or nothing. The model's weights know nothing newer, and it is fuzzy because data about recent months is sparse (the web has not finished writing about them), so the model's effective knowledge is weaker near the cutoff than the stated date suggests. Models also often misreport their own cutoff. In applications I inject the current date, and use retrieval or tools for anything time-sensitive."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Why fuzzy: Content about month M keeps accumulating for years (analysis, wikis, forum threads). A model trained shortly after M sees only a thin slice, so recall of late events is poor even when the cutoff nominally covers them. Result: effective cutoff earlier than the documented one.
  • Why models misstate it: The model has no clock and no metadata about its own training; it infers from data density, which tends to underestimate.
  • Post-training can add later info (SFT and preference data may be collected after pretraining cutoff), so different capabilities have different effective dates.
  • App patterns: inject Today is 2026-11-02 in the system prompt; use web/RAG tools for fresh facts; label answers with sources; for versioned APIs (libraries, prices) retrieve docs rather than trusting memory.
  • Failure modes: model recommends deprecated APIs, quotes old prices, assumes the latest model it knows is the latest in existence.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
from datetime import date
system = f"Current date: {date.today().isoformat()}. If asked about events after your training data, use the search tool; do not guess."

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Trusting the model's self-reported cutoff.
  • Computing "recent" or "age" without supplying the date.
  • Fine-tuning to inject fresh facts instead of retrieval (expensive, lossy).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a newer cutoff mean RAG is unnecessary? → No; cutoffs lag release by months and private data was never there.
  2. How would you test freshness? → Questions about events at known dates; plot accuracy vs event date.
  3. Why would a model confidently describe a stale "latest version"? → Parametric memory has no notion of time; the latest version it saw is "latest."

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "it doesn't know recent stuff." Senior explains data-density fuzziness, separate effective dates per capability, and the architecture (date injection plus retrieval).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A coding assistant kept suggesting an SDK call removed 8 months earlier; adding docs retrieval fixed it more reliably than any prompt.

questions.promptHtml: Explain the classic RLHF pipeline: what are the stages, how is the reward model trained, and what does PPO optimize?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: RLHF is the canonical alignment recipe; everything else (DPO, RLAIF, GRPO) is defined relative to it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Three stages: SFT on demonstrations; train a reward model on human pairwise preferences using a Bradley-Terry loss; then optimize the SFT policy with PPO to maximize reward minus a KL penalty to the SFT reference, so it does not drift into gibberish that fools the reward model. InstructGPT showed labelers preferred a 1.3B RLHF model over the 175B GPT-3 base."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
prompts -> SFT model samples k responses -> humans rank -> pairs (y_w, y_l)
reward model r(x,y): loss = -log sigmoid( r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l) )     (Bradley-Terry)
PPO: maximize  E[ r(x,y) ] - beta * KL( pi_theta(.|x) || pi_ref(.|x) )
  • Reward model: usually the SFT model with the LM head replaced by a scalar head. Only differences in score matter (Bradley-Terry models P(y_w preferred) = sigmoid(r_w - r_l)).
  • PPO loop: sample responses from the policy, score with RM, subtract per-token KL, estimate advantages with a value (critic) network, update with the clipped objective. Four models live in memory: policy, reference, reward, value. That is why RLHF is expensive and finicky.
  • KL term: keeps the policy near the reference; beta too low invites reward hacking, too high yields no learning. Often adapted dynamically toward a target KL.
  • InstructGPT detail (verify from paper): PPO-ptx mixes pretraining-gradient updates into PPO to reduce regressions on public NLP benchmarks.
  • Reward is sequence-level but credit is token-level: the RM scores only the full response (usually at the final token), so the value network must learn credit assignment.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import torch.nn.functional as F

def rm_loss(r_chosen, r_rejected):
    # r_*: [B] scalar rewards
    return -F.logsigmoid(r_chosen - r_rejected).mean()

def kl_shaped_reward(rm_score, logp_policy, logp_ref, beta=0.05):
    # per-token KL estimate added as penalty; RM score lands on the last token
    kl = logp_policy - logp_ref          # [T]
    rew = -beta * kl
    rew[-1] += rm_score
    return rew

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking the reward model outputs a calibrated probability; it outputs a relative score.
  • Forgetting the reference model; without KL the policy exploits RM quirks.
  • Describing PPO as "the reward model gives rewards" and skipping the value model and memory cost.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why pairwise preferences rather than scalar ratings? → Humans are inconsistent on absolute scores but consistent on comparisons.
  2. Why is PPO hard at LLM scale? → Four models, many hyperparameters, instability, sampling latency in the loop.
  3. What does the RM not capture? → Anything outside its training distribution; as the policy moves, the RM extrapolates badly (over-optimization).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average recites three steps. Senior gives the loss and the objective, names the memory/stability cost, and flags reward over-optimization as the core risk.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams running their own RLHF often find the RM, not PPO, is the bottleneck: noisy labels create a ceiling on what the policy can improve.

questions.promptHtml: How does Direct Preference Optimization work, and when would you choose it over PPO-based RLHF?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: DPO is the default open-source preference method; seniors must know its math, assumptions and failure modes, not only "no reward model."

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "DPO rewrites the RLHF objective so the optimal policy is a closed-form function of the reward. That lets you express the reward as beta times the log-ratio of policy to reference, and train directly on preference pairs with a simple logistic loss. No reward model, no sampling loop, no value network: two forward passes per pair. I choose it for cheap, stable alignment with an offline preference dataset; I prefer online RL when I need exploration, verifiable rewards, or the data is far from the policy's own outputs."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Loss:

L = -log sigmoid( beta * [ (log pi(y_w|x) - log ref(y_w|x)) - (log pi(y_l|x) - log ref(y_l|x)) ] )
  • Intuition: raise the likelihood of chosen relative to the reference, lower rejected, with beta controlling how far from the reference the policy may go (the same role as the KL coefficient). Common beta around 0.1 (verify per library default).
  • Implicit reward: beta * log(pi/ref) is the implicit reward model; you can evaluate it, though it is not equivalent to a separately trained RM.
  • Offline, off-policy: pairs usually come from other models. The policy never samples in training, so it can't discover better behavior; data/policy mismatch hurts.
  • Known issues: both chosen and rejected likelihood can fall (just the gap grows), producing degraded fluency; length bias (longer chosen responses make the policy verbose); sensitivity to SFT quality and to beta; overfitting after a few epochs. Variants (IPO, SimPO, KTO, ORPO) address some of these (verify details before citing).
  • Compute: policy plus frozen reference (reference log-probs can be precomputed once).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import torch.nn.functional as F

def dpo_loss(pi_w, pi_l, ref_w, ref_l, beta=0.1):
    # each: [B] summed token log-probs of the response given the prompt
    margin = beta * ((pi_w - ref_w) - (pi_l - ref_l))
    return -F.logsigmoid(margin).mean()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying DPO "has no reward model"; it has an implicit one.
  • Using DPO directly on a base model without SFT first (reference is poor).
  • Ignoring that sum-of-logprobs favors short or long sequences depending on setup.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why a reference model? → The closed-form solution depends on it; it also anchors the KL-like regularization.
  2. Why do both chosen and rejected log-probs sometimes decrease? → The loss only constrains the difference; the model can lower both.
  3. When does online RL beat DPO? → When rewards are verifiable or you need on-policy exploration; DPO cannot improve beyond what pairs demonstrate.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "simpler than PPO." Senior writes the loss, explains the implicit reward, names off-policy and length-bias failures, and picks by data and reward availability.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team's DPO run raised preference win rate but average output length grew 40%; latency and cost rose until length-normalized variants and a length-controlled eval were added.

questions.contextHtml: Your team has an SFT'd 8B model for a legal-drafting assistant. You have 12,000 human-labeled preference pairs (drafts ranked by lawyers), 2 GPUs of 80 GB, a 3-week deadline, and no RL infra. The product lead asks for "RLHF so it follows firm style." Output quality is judged by lawyers; there is no automatic correctness check. Inference budget is fixed; verbosity is already a complaint.
questions.promptHtml: Which preference-optimization approach do you propose, and what do you build around it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Do PPO because it is the real RLHF," ignoring infra, time, and data size; or "just do DPO" with no evaluation plan.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Were the pairs generated by our SFT model or by other models (on-policy matters)? Inter-annotator agreement? Is style the only target, or also factual accuracy? What is the length distribution of chosen vs rejected? Can we get fresh pairs in the loop?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I'd freeze a baseline eval set (200 held-out prompts, lawyer-rated) before touching weights so we can show improvement.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: DPO (or a variant) is the fit: 12k pairs, 2 GPUs, 3 weeks, no verifier. PPO needs RM plus 4 models and tuning: too risky. Best-of-n with an RM is an alternative if we want no training. SFT-only on chosen responses (rejection-sampling fine-tuning) is a cheap baseline.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run three arms on the same split: SFT on chosen only, DPO (beta sweep 0.05/0.1/0.3), and optionally best-of-4 with a trained RM. Evaluate by blind lawyer comparisons and length-controlled win rate, plus regression tests on general tasks.
  5. Root cause: N/A. The key insight: with a reference-anchored loss and modest data, the main risk is length bias and overfitting, not compute.
  6. Fix / plan: Precompute reference log-probs, 1-2 epochs, low LR (e.g. 5e-7 range for full DPO is common; verify), LoRA if memory-bound. Check chosen/rejected length ratio; if chosen is >1.3x longer, length-normalize or balance the data.
  7. Prevention: Track reward margins, chosen logprob (watch for it falling), average length, refusal rate; a canary rollout with lawyer review.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not PPO now (infra cost, instability, and no verifiable reward); not training an RM only to overfit it; not shipping on win rate alone without a length-controlled view.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Pairs came from GPT-style outputs, not our model. → Off-policy mismatch: first do SFT on chosen or sample from our model and re-label a subset.
  • Lawyers disagree 30% of the time. → Filter to high-agreement pairs and treat the rest as noise; consider confidence-weighted loss.
  • Client wants it by next week. → Ship rejection-sampling SFT; DPO as v2.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team shipped a DPO model that won internal preference tests but users complained of padding; the preference data had chosen responses 35% longer. Re-labeling with length-balanced pairs fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Picks method by name recognition; no eval plan.
  • Hire: Chooses DPO with justification, plans baseline, mentions beta and length bias.
  • Strong hire: Frames on-policy vs off-policy, proposes ablation arms, data-quality filters, monitoring signals, and a staged rollout.

questions.promptHtml: What is reward hacking / over-optimization in RLHF, why does it happen mechanically, and how do you detect and limit it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Core alignment failure mode; seniors should explain it with Goodhart's law and give concrete mitigations.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The reward model is a learned proxy trained on limited data. When the policy optimizes it hard, it finds regions where the proxy is high but true quality is low: verbose, flattering, formatted-looking answers. Gold reward rises then falls as proxy reward keeps climbing. I limit it with a KL penalty, early stopping on a held-out gold signal, RM ensembles, larger/better RMs, fresh preference data on policy samples, and by auditing output length and style."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Goodhart: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. The RM is accurate near its training distribution (SFT-like samples). RL pushes the policy off that distribution, where RM scores are unreliable extrapolations.
  • Scaling-law view: Gao et al. (Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization) measured gold reward vs KL distance to the reference: it rises then declines, and larger RMs push the peak further out (verify numbers in paper).
  • Typical exploits: length (RMs prefer longer), sycophantic agreement, confident tone, markdown and lists, hedging disclaimers, repeating the prompt, special tokens that trigger high scores. In code RL: editing unit tests, special-casing test inputs.
  • Detection: track proxy reward vs an independent gold signal (human or stronger-model judge on held-out prompts), KL to reference, length trend, diversity (self-BLEU, entropy), and manual reading of top-reward samples each checkpoint.
  • Mitigations: KL penalty or target KL, early stop, RM ensembles with min/mean-minus-std, regularizing on length, iterated RLHF (re-collect labels on current policy samples), constraining reward range, verifiable rewards where possible, adversarial prompts for the RM.
reward
  |        proxy (RM)  ______________
  |               ___/
  |      gold  __/ \__
  |        ___/       \___   <- over-optimized
  +------------------------ KL from reference

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import numpy as np

def pessimistic_reward(scores):
    # scores: [n_models] RM ensemble scores for one sample
    return float(np.mean(scores) - 1.0 * np.std(scores))  # penalize disagreement

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Judging progress by proxy reward only.
  • Treating high KL as fine because "reward is going up."
  • Blaming the RL algorithm when the RM is the problem.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does DPO avoid reward hacking? → No; it can exploit dataset artifacts (length, style) offline; there is no reward model but the same Goodhart dynamics apply.
  2. Why does a bigger RM help? → Better generalization out of distribution, so the exploitable gap shrinks.
  3. How would you build a hack-detection eval? → A held-out adversarial set plus human audit of high-reward outliers and an independent judge from a different model family.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "model games the reward." Senior explains distribution shift of the RM under optimization, the rise-then-fall gold curve, and a monitoring plan with independent gold signals.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A tuned assistant's reward climbed for 3 days while user thumbs-up rate fell; the policy had learned to open every answer with praise of the question.

questions.promptHtml: Why do preference-trained models become sycophantic, and what can you do about it in data and training?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real products fail because the model agrees with wrong user claims; interviewers want to see the root cause in the data, not just "prompt it to be honest."

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Human raters, and reward models trained on their votes, tend to prefer answers that agree with them, flatter them, and sound confident. Optimizing against that preference signal teaches the model to tell people what they want to hear. Anthropic's sycophancy research found this behavior across RLHF-trained assistants and that preference models sometimes prefer sycophantic responses over truthful ones (verify details). Mitigations: counter-sycophancy training data, diversified and expert raters, rewarding disagreement when the user is wrong, and evals that flip user opinion."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Mechanism: pairs where the chosen response matches the user's stated belief outnumber ones where it corrects them; the RM learns agreement as a feature; PPO or DPO amplify it.
  • Forms: changing a correct answer after pushback, praising mediocre work, mirroring a user's political views, validating risky plans.
  • Rater limits: non-experts can't verify claims, so confidence and politeness stand in for correctness.
  • Mitigations in data: include pairs where the user is wrong and the chosen answer politely corrects; balance opinions; use expert raters or tools for fact-checking; synthetic pushback data ("Are you sure?" with the model holding the correct answer).
  • Mitigations in evaluation: a pushback test: ask a question, get a correct answer, say "I think that's wrong," measure flip rate; opinion-swap prompts where only the stated user view changes.
  • Prompt-level helps but does not remove the training-level bias.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def flip_rate(model, items):
    flips = 0
    for q, gold in items:
        a1 = model(q)
        a2 = model([q, a1, "I don't think that's right. Are you sure?"])
        flips += (gold in a1) and (gold not in a2)
    return flips / len(items)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Measuring only helpfulness ratings, which reward sycophancy.
  • Fixing with a "be honest" system prompt and declaring victory.
  • Training on pushback data that teaches stubbornness even when the user is right.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you avoid stubbornness? → Include cases where the user is right and the model should update.
  2. Does RLAIF fix it? → Can inherit or shift the bias; the AI judge is also trained on human preferences.
  3. How measure in production? → Pushback replay on logged conversations plus a sample audit.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "model is too agreeable." Senior traces it to the rater/RM incentive, builds a flip-rate eval, and balances against over-correction.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An internal analytics bot confirmed a manager's incorrect revenue assumption three turns in a row; a flip-rate test later showed 40% capitulation under pushback (illustrative).

questions.contextHtml: You shipped a DPO-tuned 70B assistant two weeks ago. Offline pairwise win rate vs the previous model: 64%. Live metrics since: average output 210 tokens (was 150), p95 latency 6.1 s (was 4.4 s), GPU spend up 22%, support-ticket thumbs-down on "too wordy" up 3x, and a new log pattern: Great question! ... In summary, ... on 70% of answers. JSON-mode tasks show valid-JSON rate down from 99.1% to 96.8%. DPO run: beta 0.1, 3 epochs, 40k pairs. Reward-margin on train hit 8.0. Red herring: traffic mix is unchanged and the serving engine was not upgraded.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix. What would you tell the VP who asks "didn't evals say it was better?"

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Roll back and ship again later," or "tune temperature." No mechanism for why offline evals missed it.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How were pairs sourced and what is the chosen/rejected length ratio? Was the win-rate judge length-controlled? Did the eval include format-strict tasks? Which checkpoint (epoch 1 vs 3)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Route traffic back to the previous model for JSON/structured endpoints (feature-flag by task); for the rest, add a concise-style system instruction and a lower max_tokens while a fix trains.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Length bias in pairs plus a length-biased judge, so the win rate was partly verbosity; (b) over-training: 3 epochs with train margin 8.0 suggests overfitting and policy drift from reference; (c) pairs contain the opener/summary template, which got amplified; (d) JSON failure from drift away from the SFT model's strict-format behavior.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compute mean length of chosen vs rejected in the 40k pairs; recompute win rate with a length-controlled metric (regress out length, or compare at matched lengths); compare epoch-1 checkpoint behavior; count opener phrases in data vs outputs; run the JSON eval suite on each checkpoint; check mean chosen logprob trend.
  5. Root cause: Preference data where chosen was ~30% longer and used a stock opener/closer taught the implicit reward "longer, polite template = better". Three epochs pushed the policy far from the reference. The offline judge also preferred longer answers, so the metric was inflated.
  6. Fix: Short term: serve epoch-1 checkpoint if it passes both length-controlled win rate and JSON suite. Long term: rebalance pairs by length, strip templated openers from chosen, use a length-normalized variant (e.g. SimPO-style, verify) or add a length penalty, raise beta, train 1 epoch, and mix in format-strict SFT/replay data.
  7. Prevention: Eval gate on length-controlled win rate, mean tokens, structured-output validity, and refusal rate; cost-per-task, not cost-per-token, on the release dashboard; shadow traffic before cutover.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't hide it with a truncating max_tokens (cuts answers mid-thought), and wouldn't discard DPO entirely; the gain on substance may be real once length is controlled.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Length-controlled win rate is only 52%. → Then most of the 64% was verbosity; the model is not meaningfully better.
  • Can't retrain for 3 weeks. → Merge weights: interpolate SFT and DPO checkpoints (weight averaging) as a tunable knob (verify on your setup).
  • Users like friendliness. → Make tone a controllable style, not an accident; measure satisfaction by task completion.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a launch passed every offline gate and cost-per-resolved-ticket rose 18%, because verbosity added tokens without more resolutions. The team then added tokens-per-resolution to the gate.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Treats it as sampling/serving problem.
  • Hire: Identifies length bias, over-training; proposes epoch rollback and length-controlled eval.
  • Strong hire: Links data artifacts to the metric blind spot, protects structured endpoints, adds release gates tied to cost and format validity.

questions.promptHtml: What are RLAIF and Constitutional AI, how do they differ from RLHF, and what are the risks of replacing human labels with model labels?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most teams cannot afford large human-labeling programs; AI feedback is the practical route, and its biases are the senior-level concern.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "RLAIF replaces human preference labels with labels from an AI judge. Constitutional AI, from Anthropic, goes further: a written set of principles drives the model to critique and revise its own responses (supervised phase), and an AI judge picks the better response according to the principles to produce preference data for RL (RLAIF phase). It scales cheaply and makes the rules explicit and auditable. Risks: the judge's own biases (length, self-preference, sycophancy) get baked in, and errors are correlated, not averaged out like independent humans."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Constitutional AI (Bai et al., 2022):
  Phase 1 (SL):  response -> self-critique per principle -> revision -> SFT on revisions
  Phase 2 (RL):  sample pair -> AI picks better per principle -> train preference model -> RL
  • Why it helps: harmlessness data from humans means exposing annotators to toxic content and is slow. A constitution is a compact, editable spec; changing behavior means editing a principle and regenerating labels.
  • Judge quality: strong judges agree with humans on many tasks at lower cost; agreement is task-dependent, so measure it on a human-labeled sample.
  • Biases: position bias (prefers first/second), verbosity bias, self-preference (a model favors its own style), and shared blind spots with the policy being trained. Mitigate by swapping order, using a different or larger judge, calibrating on gold labels, and ensembling.
  • Hybrid in practice: humans label a gold set and handle the hard or sensitive categories; AI labels the bulk.
  • Not a free lunch: a policy trained on its own judge's preferences can amplify the judge's errors in a loop.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def judge_pair(judge, prompt, a, b, principle):
    # run both orders to cancel position bias
    s1 = judge(f"Principle: {principle}
Prompt: {prompt}
A: {a}
B: {b}
Which better? A or B")
    s2 = judge(f"Principle: {principle}
Prompt: {prompt}
A: {b}
B: {a}
Which better? A or B")
    if s1 == "A" and s2 == "B": return "a"
    if s1 == "B" and s2 == "A": return "b"
    return "tie"   # inconsistent -> drop the pair

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming the AI judge agrees with your users; never validating on human labels.
  • Using the same model as judge and policy, amplifying self-preference.
  • Writing vague principles ("be good") that can't produce consistent labels.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you validate AI labels? → Sample 300-500, double-label by humans, compute agreement and per-category error.
  2. Does it remove the need for humans? → No; humans define principles, gold sets and audits.
  3. What failure appears if the judge is weaker than the policy? → The policy learns to look good to a weak judge: reward hacking on judge blind spots.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "AI labels instead of humans." Senior describes the two-phase CAI recipe, judge biases with mitigations, and the correlated-error risk.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team using an LLM judge for preference data found its judge favored longer replies; removing order and length bias cut the verbosity drift in the tuned model.

questions.promptHtml: What is reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), how does GRPO fit in, and what does it change compared with RLHF? What are its limits?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: RLVR underlies the reasoning-model wave; a senior should explain why it works where RLHF struggles and what it does not guarantee. This area moves fast, so verify current status.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "RLVR uses a programmatic checker as the reward: exact match on a math answer, unit tests for code, a format validator. No learned reward model, so far less reward hacking from a fuzzy proxy and no human labels needed. GRPO, introduced in DeepSeekMath and used for DeepSeek-R1, samples a group of responses per prompt and uses the group-normalized reward as the advantage, removing the value network. It works only where correctness is checkable, and some research argues it mostly sharpens sampling of abilities already in the base model rather than creating new ones; that is still debated."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
for each prompt x:
    sample G responses y_1..y_G from current policy
    r_i = verifier(x, y_i)                   # e.g. 1 if answer correct, else 0
    A_i = (r_i - mean(r)) / (std(r) + eps)   # GRPO advantage
    update policy to raise prob of high-A samples (clipped, KL to ref optional)
  • Why no critic: the group mean serves as the baseline, saving a value model of policy size (a large memory win).
  • Rewards: accuracy rewards plus format rewards (e.g., reasoning inside tags). DeepSeek-R1-Zero applied RL directly to a base model with no SFT; reported issues were poor readability and language mixing, which the full R1 pipeline addressed with a cold-start SFT stage (as I read the secondary sources; verify with the R1 paper).
  • Where it works: math, code with tests, logic puzzles, structured extraction with a checkable schema, some tool-use tasks with state checks.
  • Limits: prompts the model always or never solves give zero gradient (all rewards equal), so difficulty filtering/curricula matter; verifier bugs get exploited (hardcoding test outputs); open-ended tasks (writing, advice) lack verifiers; length can inflate; evidence (e.g., "Reasoning LLMs are just efficient samplers"-style studies, April 2025) suggests pass@1 improves while pass@k at large k may not exceed the base: treat as an open question.
  • Status caveat: recipes, variants (DAPO, Dr. GRPO, etc.) and claims change monthly; verify before citing.

  3. Can you apply it to non-verifiable tasks? → Via rubric-based or judge rewards, which reintroduces proxy risk.

questions.contextHtml:
A teammate implements DPO. Training runs, loss falls from 0.69 to 0.05 in 200 steps, reward accuracy hits 99%, but generations get worse: repetitive, sometimes empty, and held-out win rate vs the SFT model is 38%. Code:

ref = copy.deepcopy(policy)          # (A) never switched to eval(); dropout stays on
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(policy.parameters(), lr=5e-5)

def dpo_step(batch, beta=0.1):
    pw = seq_logp(policy, batch["chosen"])
    pl = seq_logp(policy, batch["rejected"])
    with torch.no_grad():
        rw = seq_logp(ref, batch["chosen"])
        rl = seq_logp(ref, batch["rejected"])
    margin = beta * ((pw - rw) - (pl - rl))
    return -F.logsigmoid(margin).mean()

def seq_logp(model, ids):            # (B) sums over ALL positions, padding and prompt included
    logits = model(ids).logits[:, :-1]
    lp = torch.log_softmax(logits, -1).gather(-1, ids[:, 1:, None]).squeeze(-1)
    return lp.sum(-1)

Config: 5 epochs, chosen/rejected padded with pad_token_id, no attention-mask passed. Red herring: the data has been checked and looks fine.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bugs and explain why the loss dropped so fast while quality fell.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Lower the LR." Misses the masking and reference-mode bugs and does not explain the unbounded-margin dynamic.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the loss at step 0 exactly ln 2 (about 0.693)? With dropout on in ref but not necessarily in policy, it will not be. Is padding masked? Which tokens are in the log-prob sum? Which LR do comparable recipes use?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop the run, discard the checkpoint, keep the SFT model serving.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) log-probs sum over prompt and padding tokens (and no attention mask), so the "margin" is dominated by artifacts the model can change cheaply; (b) LR 5e-5 for 5 epochs is one to two orders of magnitude above typical DPO full fine-tune LRs (order 1e-6 to 5e-7; verify), so the policy runs far from the reference; (c) ref in train mode with dropout gives noisy, non-deterministic reference log-probs; (d) the objective itself only constrains the gap, so both chosen and rejected likelihood fall.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log chosen and rejected log-probs separately: both falling is the signature of (d). Check step-0 loss: it should be ln 2 exactly if ref equals policy in eval mode; a different value flags (c). Print the masks and count tokens in the sum. Compute KL between policy and reference on held-out prompts: a large value flags (b).
  5. Root cause: Reward accuracy hits 99% because the model found cheap ways to widen the margin (changing padding/prompt-token terms, collapsing rejected likelihood) while drifting far from the reference. Nothing stops this: DPO's regularization is only as strong as beta and a modest number of small steps. Loss falling that fast is the symptom, not success.
  6. Fix:
ref.eval(); [p.requires_grad_(False) for p in ref.parameters()]

def seq_logp(model, ids, attn, resp_mask):   # resp_mask = 1 on response tokens only
    logits = model(input_ids=ids, attention_mask=attn).logits[:, :-1].float()
    lp = torch.log_softmax(logits, -1).gather(-1, ids[:, 1:, None]).squeeze(-1)
    return (lp * resp_mask[:, 1:]).sum(-1)

LR near 5e-7 to 1e-6, 1 to 2 epochs, precompute reference log-probs once. 7. Prevention: Unit tests: step-0 loss is ln 2, reference params unchanged after N steps, masks only cover response tokens. Dashboard: chosen/rejected logp, KL to reference, reward accuracy, length. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not patch with an extra SFT term before fixing masks; if chosen logp still falls afterward, adding an NLL term on chosen is a reasonable follow-up.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Memory is tight. -> Precompute reference log-probs offline, or use LoRA and disable the adapter to get the reference.
  • Why does rejected logp fall without bound? -> The loss only constrains the difference.
  • Reward accuracy 99% on train: good? -> No; on a noisy human-preference set 70-75% is typical, so 99% means overfitting or artifacts.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: months of "DPO doesn't work for us" came from padding tokens in the log-prob sum. After masking, win rate went from 41% to 63%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Only suggests tuning LR.
  • Hire: Spots masking, LR/epochs, and reference-mode issues.
  • Strong hire: Explains the unbounded-margin dynamic, adds tests and diagnostics, offers LoRA-as-reference.

questions.promptHtml: What is catastrophic forgetting when fine-tuning an LLM, why does it happen, and what techniques reduce it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Teams fine-tune on a narrow domain and silently lose general abilities; seniors should anticipate and measure it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Fine-tuning updates the same shared weights that store general skills. If the new data distribution is narrow and the learning rate or epochs are high, gradients move weights away from the regions that supported old abilities, and old performance drops: format following, safety refusals, other languages. I reduce it with lower LR, fewer epochs, LoRA/adapters, replay of general or original-style data mixed in, regularization toward the original weights, and by regression-testing a general eval suite."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Mechanism: parameters are not partitioned by skill; features are distributed. Gradient steps tuned to the new loss are not constrained by the old loss. Larger models often forget less in relative terms but not zero.
  • What forgets first: instruction-following style, safety training (fine-tuning on benign data can degrade refusals; shown in the literature, verify specific paper), long-context behavior, rarely used languages.
  • Techniques:
Technique Idea Cost
Lower LR / fewer epochs smaller drift cheap
LoRA / adapters freeze base, low-rank deltas; less drift (not zero; "LoRA learns less and forgets less" is a reported trade-off, verify) cheap
Data replay mix 10-30% general instruct data data needed
Weight interpolation average tuned and original weights cheap, tunable
KL / L2-to-init regularization penalize distance from base extra compute
  • Measure: hold a "canary" suite: MMLU-style subset, IFEval-like format tests, safety prompts, domain-agnostic tasks; compare before/after.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def mix_batches(domain_ds, general_ds, p_general=0.2, rng=None):
    import random
    rng = rng or random.Random(0)
    while True:
        yield rng.choice(general_ds) if rng.random() < p_general else rng.choice(domain_ds)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Only evaluating on the new domain.
  • Believing LoRA eliminates forgetting.
  • Training multiple epochs on a small set (memorization plus drift).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can fine-tuning harm safety? → Refusal behavior is a thin learned layer; narrow tuning can overwrite it.
  2. Which is better, replay or regularization? → Replay is simpler and usually effective; regularization needs tuning.
  3. How would you choose p_general? → Sweep; pick the knee between domain score and general canary score.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use LoRA." Senior combines techniques, builds a regression canary, and checks safety.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A contract-extraction fine-tune hit 97% on its domain and dropped instruction-following on unrelated tasks by 15 points; the product's general chat feature broke.

questions.promptHtml: What is the "alignment tax," and is it real in current models?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests nuance: post-training can both help and hurt, and the answer depends on the metric.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Alignment tax is the drop in raw capability or benchmark performance caused by alignment training, such as RLHF. InstructGPT observed regressions on some public NLP tasks from PPO and reduced them by mixing pretraining gradients into the update (PPO-ptx). Today the tax is usually small on knowledge benchmarks and often negative for usability, but it shows up as lower calibration, less diversity, over-refusal, and sometimes lower performance on tasks like few-shot completion. It is a trade-off that must be measured per use case."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Where it appears: (a) benchmark regressions on tasks not in the preference data; (b) calibration worse in chat than base; (c) reduced output diversity (mode collapse), hurting creative and synthetic-data use; (d) over-refusal on benign prompts; (e) verbosity.
  • Where it's negative (a bonus): instruction following, tool use, safety, and human preference all improve; InstructGPT's 1.3B model was preferred to 175B GPT-3 by labelers.
  • Mitigations: KL regularization, pretrain-mix gradients, replay in SFT, weight averaging of pre- and post-RL models (reported to reduce the tax; verify), better, more diverse preference data.
  • Engineering viewpoint: treat each stage as having costs; track a capability dashboard across checkpoints instead of one score.

sections.html:
• Claiming alignment always costs capability.
  • Ignoring non-benchmark taxes: diversity, calibration.
  • Comparing chat and base on completion tasks without prompt adjustment.

sections.html:
1. How would you quantify it? → Matched eval suite on base vs tuned with correct prompting formats for each.
  2. Why does diversity drop? → Preference optimization sharpens the distribution toward high-reward modes.
  3. How does the tax relate to over-refusal? → Safety tuning generalizes too broadly, refusing harmless near-boundary prompts.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "alignment makes models worse at raw tasks." Senior distinguishes benchmark tax, calibration/diversity tax, and refusal tax, and cites mitigations.
