sections.html: A team generating synthetic data with an instruct model got near-duplicate outputs; switching to a base model with few-shot prompts restored diversity.

questions.contextHtml: Your company fine-tuned a 13B chat model with an extra safety dataset (6,000 refusal examples, 2 epochs) for a healthcare-adjacent product. After launch, support sees complaints: the model refuses "What is the maximum safe dose of ibuprofen?" and "How do I kill a Python process?". Over 4 weeks, refusal rate on benign eval prompts went from 2% to 14%, while red-team attack success fell from 20% to 3%. Log excerpt: assistant: I'm sorry, but I can't help with that request. on 9% of 120k weekly queries. Red herring: system prompt unchanged for 2 months.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: what went wrong, how do you measure and fix it, what process change prevents recurrence?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Remove the safety data" or "tell the model not to refuse"; no measurement of the safety/helpfulness trade-off.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What did the refusal set contain: only harmful prompts, or near-miss contrasts? Was a benign over-refusal eval part of the gate? Did refusals concentrate on keywords ("kill", "dose")? Which checkpoint?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back to the pre-safety checkpoint with an input/output moderation layer for the high-risk categories, then iterate.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Refusal set lacks contrastive benign twins, so the model learned surface keyword triggers; (b) refusal data too uniform, dominating the style; (c) 2 epochs over-fit the template; (d) no replay of helpful data.
  4. How I'd verify each: Cluster refused benign prompts by n-gram; measure refusal vs presence of trigger words; build XSTest-style benign-but-edgy prompts (verify availability); compare checkpoints; check ratio of refusal to helpful examples.
  5. Root cause: Safety data without hard negatives teaches lexical triggers, a classic over-generalization: the safety gate measured attack success only.
  6. Fix: Add benign contrast pairs (same words, benign intent) with helpful answers; mix safety data into a general SFT set (e.g., 5% refusals); add graded responses (safe completion with caveats rather than flat refusal); train 1 epoch; re-evaluate.
  7. Prevention: Two-sided gate: attack success rate and benign refusal rate, both with thresholds; weekly sampled review of refusals in production; category-specific policy for medical info.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not zero refusals (legal risk), not purely prompt-based fixes (training-level behavior resists), not removing red-team coverage.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Compliance wants refusal rate on harmful prompts to stay below 5% attack success. → Keep the metric as a hard constraint and optimize helpfulness inside it.
  • Can the classifier front layer replace training changes? → It can reduce risk but adds latency/cost and has its own false positives.
  • Users complain only in one language. → Safety data was probably English-heavy; add multilingual contrast sets.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a launch gate reported attack success 3% and was celebrated; the medical team found a nurse-facing tool refusing dosage questions for a week.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests deleting safety data or prompt hacks only.
  • Hire: Diagnoses missing hard negatives; two-sided metrics.
  • Strong hire: Adds contrastive data, graded responses, monitoring, language coverage, compliance trade-off.

questions.promptHtml: When is training on model-generated data safe and useful, and what is model collapse? How do you build a synthetic pipeline that avoids it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Synthetic data is now a staple of post-training; seniors must know where it helps, where it degrades, and how to control it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Synthetic data is great when a filter or verifier injects information the generator did not have: correctness checks, tests, stronger-teacher distillation, human-curated seeds. It is dangerous when a model is trained recursively on its own unfiltered outputs: Shumailov et al. showed the tails of the distribution vanish over generations, a degradation they called model collapse. Mitigations: keep real data in the mix (accumulating rather than replacing helps), filter hard, diversify generators and prompts, and measure diversity, not only quality."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Why collapse happens: each generation samples from a learned approximation of the previous distribution. Sampling under-represents rare events (low-probability tails), estimation error compounds, and variance shrinks. After several generations rare content is gone and outputs get repetitive. The paper shows it for VAEs, GMMs and LLMs (abstract level; I did not verify experimental details).
  • Replace vs accumulate: collapse is strongest when each generation trains only on the previous generation's output; work on accumulating real plus synthetic data reports it can be avoided or bounded (verify the specific paper before citing).
  • Why synthetic works in practice: (1) distillation from a stronger teacher (information flows in); (2) rejection sampling with verifiers (math answers, unit tests); (3) rewriting and augmentation of real data (paraphrase, formatting); (4) self-instruct style bootstrapping with filtering; (5) persona/seed diversification.
  • Failure modes: style homogenization, error amplification (wrong but fluent samples), inherited biases from the teacher, licensing issues if the teacher's terms forbid training competitors (check provider terms), and contamination of eval sets.
  • Controls: dedup synthetic data (near-duplicates are common), embed-and-cluster to measure coverage, mix ratio caps, hold out real data eval, track n-gram diversity and entropy across rounds.
gen0 real -> model1 -> samples -> model2 -> samples -> model3 ...
tails:  |======|---|--    |====|-     |==|       (rare modes disappear)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
from collections import Counter

def distinct_n(texts, n=3):
    grams = Counter()
    total = 0
    for t in texts:
        toks = t.split()
        for i in range(len(toks) - n + 1):
            grams[tuple(toks[i:i+n])] += 1
            total += 1
    return len(grams) / max(total, 1)   # falling across rounds = diversity loss

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Equating "synthetic" with "bad" or with "free quality."
  • Filtering only on fluency, not correctness.
  • Generating all data from one prompt template at temperature 0.7 and wondering why it is repetitive.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does rejection sampling not collapse? → The verifier adds external information that selects correct samples.
  2. What if the teacher is the same size as the student? → Gains come only via filtering/verification or larger compute at generation time (best-of-n, tools).
  3. How do you measure collapse early? → Diversity metrics and a real-data held-out loss across rounds.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "synthetic data can cause collapse." Senior explains the tail-loss mechanism, the replace vs accumulate distinction, and when external information makes synthetic data work.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team iterated self-training three rounds on a support-bot corpus; ticket categories with under 1% frequency stopped being handled, a tail-loss symptom.

questions.contextHtml: A PM says: "We have 400 real customer conversations about insurance claims. Generate 50,000 more with an LLM and fine-tune our 8B model so it handles claims." Budget: roughly $2,000 of API spend, 2 weeks, a small team. Teacher API cost is $3 per 1M input and $15 per 1M output tokens (illustrative). Average synthetic conversation is 900 output tokens and 400 input tokens. Compliance says no real customer PII may reach a third-party API. Held-out eval: 60 real conversations rated by claims staff.
questions.promptHtml: How do you scope and execute this? What would you push back on?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Generate 50k with GPT and train." No cost math, no diversity or verification plan, ignores PII.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does "handles claims" mean: extraction, Q&A, drafting replies, triage? What is success and who rates it? Can seeds be anonymized or synthesized from policy documents instead of real chats? Is the teacher license compatible with training our own model? What fails today?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; first establish a baseline: run the base 8B with few-shot prompts on the 60-example eval to see the gap.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) 50k is arbitrary; 2-5k diverse, verified examples may beat 50k near-duplicates; (b) the gap may be domain knowledge (policy rules) better solved by retrieval; (c) PII constraint forces de-identified seeds; (d) the eval set of 60 is small, so confidence intervals are wide.
  4. How I'd verify each: Cost math: per conversation = 4003/1M + 90015/1M = $0.0012 + $0.0135 = $0.0147; 50,000 = about $735, within budget but filtering/regeneration of rejects (assume 50% kept) doubles it to roughly $1,500. Pilot 500 samples, measure acceptance rate, diversity (distinct-n, embedding clusters), and human-rate 50 of them.
  5. Root cause: N/A. The core risk is optimizing volume instead of coverage and correctness.
  6. Plan: (1) De-identify the 400 seeds with an in-house NER/redaction step before any API call; (2) extract a taxonomy (claim types, edge cases) and sample scenario specs from it to force diversity; (3) generate with varied personas/temperatures; (4) filter with rules (policy-citation check, schema validity), a judge model on a rubric, and dedup; (5) mix with the real seeds (upweight real); (6) SFT 2 epochs with LoRA; (7) compare against few-shot and RAG baselines on the 60-set with bootstrap CI.
  7. Prevention: Version datasets with provenance (teacher model, prompt, date); log accepted vs rejected reasons; gate on held-out real data, never synthetic.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not send raw PII out; not evaluate on synthetic data; not scale to 50k before the pilot shows marginal gains; not skip license review.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Pilot shows 70% of samples are near-duplicates. → Fix the prompting (taxonomy-driven specs, persona injection), dedup, and cut volume.
  • Eval improves by 3 points on 60 examples. → Within noise; get more labeled real data or compute paired significance.
  • Legal says teacher terms forbid using outputs for training. → Use an open-weight teacher with a permissive license, check its terms.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a 40k synthetic set looked impressive; after dedup 9k unique examples remained, and a 2k curated subset matched the full-set score.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Generates and trains with no baseline or filtering.
  • Hire: Cost math, PII handling, filtering, held-out real eval.
  • Strong hire: Pushes back on 50k, proposes taxonomy-driven diversity, compares against RAG/few-shot, addresses license and CI.

questions.contextHtml: An HR-policy assistant built on a hosted chat model (provider-stated knowledge cutoff roughly 14 months ago) runs for 9,000 employees. Complaints this week: it said the "parental leave is 12 weeks" (policy changed to 16 weeks 5 months ago); it computed an employee's tenure as "4 years" when the true value is 5; and when asked "what is the latest version of our HR portal?" it named a version two releases behind. The RAG index contains the current policy PDFs (last re-indexed 6 weeks ago). Logs: top-3 retrieved chunks for the leave question include the current policy chunk at rank 2. Red herring: provider status page shows no incidents.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix. Which of these failures are cutoff problems, which are not?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The model is outdated, switch to a newer model." Lumps three different failure types together.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is today's date in the prompt? Does the prompt tell the model to prefer retrieved context over memory? Do the old and new policy chunks coexist in the index? Is there document versioning metadata? Does the answer cite sources?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a system instruction: "Answer only from provided context; if absent, say you don't know," inject the current date, and force citation of the source and its effective date.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Leave answer: parametric memory or an older policy chunk overrides retrieval (conflict between memory/old chunk and the new chunk); (b) tenure: the model has no clock, so date arithmetic used an assumed current year; (c) portal version: pure cutoff/no source, the answer came from memory; (d) stale index (6 weeks) is a minor contributor.
  4. How I'd verify each: Replay the leave query with the retrieved chunks printed; check whether an older revision of the policy is also indexed; rerun with and without the current date in the prompt; ask the version question with and without context and compare; check provider docs for the cutoff date.
  5. Root cause: Three distinct causes: knowledge conflict resolution (memory vs context), missing date grounding (tenure), and an ungrounded question about changing facts (portal version). Only the third is classic cutoff staleness.
  6. Fix: Short term: date injection, grounding instruction, supersession metadata (filter effective_to IS NULL), citation requirement. Long term: compute tenure in code via a tool rather than trusting the model, re-index on document change (event-driven), add a versions table as an authoritative source.
system = (f"Today is {date.today():%Y-%m-%d}. Answer only from the CONTEXT. "
          "If sources conflict, prefer the one with the latest effective_date. "
          "If the answer is not in CONTEXT, say you don't know.")
  1. Prevention: A freshness test set of questions with known updated answers; alerts on index age; CI check that superseded documents are excluded.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not fine-tune facts into the model (stale again next quarter); not swap models just for a newer cutoff.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did the model prefer memory over the context? → Memory had strong prior; instruction hierarchy and conflict training are imperfect; make precedence explicit and verify with tests.
  • Index re-indexed daily, still stale? → Check ingestion path and caching.
  • Employee asks about events next week. → The model should state it cannot know.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: an assistant repeatedly quoted a retired expense limit because the old PDF was still indexed with equal weight; a supersession flag fixed it in an afternoon.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "Use a newer model."
  • Hire: Separates conflict, date arithmetic, and ungrounded facts; adds date injection and grounding prompt.
  • Strong hire: Adds supersession metadata, tool-based date math, freshness test set, event-driven reindexing.

questions.contextHtml: Your assistant gets 2M conversations per month. You currently collect 8,000 human preference pairs per month at $4.50 per pair (about $36,000/month) and run DPO monthly. Leadership wants to scale the training signal 10x without a 10x bill. An experiment: an LLM judge (about $0.02 per pair, illustrative) agrees with humans 78% overall, but only 61% on the safety-sensitive and medical subsets (about 15% of traffic), and it prefers longer answers 70% of the time when lengths differ by 2x. Human inter-annotator agreement is 73%.
questions.promptHtml: Design the labeling strategy. What goes to humans, what to the AI judge, and how do you keep the pipeline honest?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Replace humans with the judge: 78% is good." Ignores category-level agreement, length bias, and the human noise ceiling.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What decisions will the data drive (DPO, RM training, eval)? Is the judge's 78% measured against consensus labels or a single annotator? Is the gold set refreshed? What is the cost of a bad safety label compared with a bad style label?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Keep human labeling unchanged for safety/medical (15% of traffic) while adding AI labels for low-risk categories under a shadow run.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The judge is good enough for style/format/helpfulness categories (agreement approaches the human 73% ceiling there), (b) fails on high-stakes categories, (c) length bias contaminates the signal and must be corrected, (d) self-preference if the judge and policy share lineage.
  4. How I'd verify each: Stratify the gold set by category; compute judge-vs-consensus agreement per stratum with bootstrapped CIs; run position-swap consistency (fraction of pairs where the judge flips with order); regress judge preference on length difference; train two DPO models (human-only vs hybrid) and compare on a held-out human-judged eval, length-controlled.
  5. Root cause: N/A. Core insight: agreement is a mean over heterogeneous strata and the noise ceiling (73%) limits what extra human labels buy.
  6. Design: Humans: 100% of safety/medical, plus a 5% audit sample of every other stratum, plus disagreement cases. AI judge: low-risk strata, after order-swapping and dropping inconsistent pairs; length-balanced sampling. Cost: humans keep roughly 8,000*(0.15) = 1,200 safety pairs plus 5% audit of 72,000 AI-labeled pairs = about 3,600, so about 4,800 human pairs = $21,600, plus 72,000 AI pairs at $0.02 = $1,440. Total about $23,000 vs $36,000 now, with 80,000 pairs (10x) in total.
  7. Prevention: Weekly judge-vs-human agreement dashboard per stratum; auto-fallback to human labeling when agreement drops below threshold; periodic judge swap/ensemble; rotate judge model versions with re-calibration.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not use one number (78%) to approve the pipeline; not let the judge label what it cannot reliably judge; not train on more AI labels without checking the downstream win rate: more noisy data is not automatically better.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Judge is the provider's model, policy is a different family. → Reduces self-preference but not shared blind spots; still validate.
  • Humans disagree 27% of the time anyway. → Use consensus or drop low-agreement pairs; label noise caps gains.
  • Judge model gets deprecated. → Re-calibrate the new judge on gold; version labels with the judge ID.

questions.promptHtml: What makes preference data good or bad? Discuss on-policy vs off-policy pairs, annotator noise, and how to curate a dataset before running DPO or RM training.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Preference-tuning outcomes depend more on data than on algorithm choice; this separates people who have actually run it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Good preference data has clear, consistent margins between chosen and rejected, covers the prompt distribution you serve, comes from outputs near the current policy (on-policy), and is free of spurious correlates like length or style. Bad data has noisy labels, tiny quality gaps, systematic artifacts, or pairs whose responses are far from anything the policy would generate. I curate by filtering by annotator agreement and margin, balancing length, deduplicating prompts, and auditing a sample by hand."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• On-policy vs off-policy: pairs sampled from the model being trained give gradient signal about its own mistakes. Pairs from other models are cheaper but the policy may assign them tiny probability; DPO then learns from inputs it would never produce (a distribution mismatch). Iterative/online DPO regenerates pairs from the current policy each round.
  • Margin and noise: if humans agree only about 70-75% of the time (common for general preference), a fraction of labels are effectively coin flips. Training on near-ties adds noise; filtering to high-margin pairs often improves results but narrows coverage.
  • Spurious features: length, markdown, politeness, confident tone. Check by regressing label on those features; balance or control.
  • Prompt coverage: pairs concentrated on easy chit-chat prompts yield a model that improves there and nothing else; stratify by task type and difficulty.
  • Pair construction: best-vs-worst of n samples with an RM or judge gives large margins (strong signal, but exposes RM biases); adjacent-rank pairs give subtle signals.
  • Contamination: keep eval prompts out; dedup prompts across splits.
Problem Symptom Fix
Length artifact outputs grow length-balanced pairs or length-normalized loss
Off-policy chosen logp falls, no gain sample from current policy
Label noise flat reward accuracy ~60% agreement filter, consensus
Narrow prompts no gain off-domain stratified sampling

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import numpy as np

def audit_pairs(pairs):
    # pairs: list of dicts with 'chosen', 'rejected', 'agree' (0-1 annotator agreement)
    len_ratio = np.array([len(p["chosen"]) / max(len(p["rejected"]), 1) for p in pairs])
    agree = np.array([p["agree"] for p in pairs])
    return {
        "chosen_longer_frac": float((len_ratio > 1).mean()),
        "median_len_ratio": float(np.median(len_ratio)),
        "low_agree_frac": float((agree < 0.6).mean()),
    }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Equating dataset size with quality.
  • Using only best-vs-worst pairs, which teaches the policy to avoid only the worst failures.
  • Not checking that chosen responses are actually good in absolute terms (both could be bad).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a reward accuracy of 99% good? → Suspicious on noisy human data; usually overfitting or artifacts.
  2. When do you prefer on-policy data? → When the policy has moved from the data's source model; it is also what online RL naturally does.
  3. How do you detect a length artifact? → Correlate label with length difference; train a length-only classifier; if it beats chance substantially, the artifact is present.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "get more pairs." Senior curates margins, controls spurious features, chooses on-policy sampling, and audits.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Pairs inherited from an older, more verbose model made a new model inherit the old model's tone, because chosen responses encoded it.

questions.contextHtml: You own a customer-support assistant built on a closed API chat model: $0.0045 per conversation, 1.2M conversations per month ($5,400/month), p95 latency 3.8 s, 91% resolution on your eval. A VP wants to "own the model" using an open-weight 8B base and cut cost 60%. You have 150k historical conversations (30k with CSAT scores), 3 engineers, 2 months, 8 GPUs available for training. The company has no RL infrastructure. The live traffic must not regress.
questions.promptHtml: Lay out the post-training plan: stages, data, evaluation and rollout. Would you commit to the cost-cut target?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Fine-tune the 8B on all 150k conversations and switch." No staged evals, no risk plan, no cost model.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which open model and license? What share of traffic is simple and repetitive vs complex? Is there PII in the history and what governs its use? What is the quality floor (resolution rate) and the acceptable regression? Do we need tool calls and structured outputs?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident. Before building, run the current eval on 8B instruct models with prompting and RAG to see the starting gap; build the eval harness first (500+ real, stratified, labeled conversations).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) An instruct 8B plus RAG plus light SFT covers the common intents at far lower cost; (b) hard tails (multi-step, ambiguous) need the large model: so a router is likely better than full replacement; (c) data quality in history is mixed (agent errors, outdated policies); (d) preference tuning adds marginal value versus SFT here.
  4. How I'd verify each: Evaluate stratified by intent and difficulty; compute resolution and safety metrics per stratum for 8B vs API model; estimate share of traffic where 8B is within 2 points.
  5. Plan: Stage 0: baseline eval. Stage 1: curate SFT data (filter to resolved, high-CSAT, policy-current conversations; redact PII; dedup; maybe 10-20k examples, plus synthetic edge cases verified by rules); SFT with LoRA or full fine-tune, 1-2 epochs, replay general data to limit forgetting. Stage 2 (optional): DPO on pairs from our model's samples ranked by high-CSAT outcome vs failure plus judge, with length control. Stage 3: shadow traffic, then 5% canary, then ramp, with an automatic fallback to the API model. Stage 4: router that sends low-confidence or complex intents to the API.
  6. Cost model: If 8B handles 70% of conversations at, say, $0.0008 each (self-hosted, verify with real throughput numbers; see the serving track) and 30% go to the API at $0.0045: blended = 0.70.0008 + 0.30.0045 = $0.00191, a 58% reduction, before fixed GPU and ops costs. Add training cost, on-call and eval overhead; compute payback period.
  7. Prevention: Per-intent regression dashboards, drift monitoring, scheduled re-evaluation when policies change, weekly review of fallback reasons.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not promise 60% before the stratified eval; not cut over fully; not use RLHF/PPO given no infra; not train on unfiltered history (teaches past agents' mistakes).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• CSAT labels are noisy and biased toward easy tickets. → Use them as a filter signal only, combined with resolution outcome, and audit.
  • 8B misses 8 points on complex intents. → Route them; consider a larger open model or distillation from the API model where licensing allows.
  • API provider cuts price 50% next quarter. → Re-run the cost model; the router and eval harness keep both options open.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team replaced 100% of traffic after a good average score, and discovered refund-policy errors in a long-tail intent that represented 4% of volume but most escalations. A router and per-intent gates restored it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: One-shot fine-tune and cutover.
  • Hire: Staged plan, evaluation before training, rollout with fallback, cost math.
  • Strong hire: Routing instead of replacement, careful data curation (filters, PII, license), explains why DPO is optional, includes fixed costs and per-stratum gates.
